cards.title: Product validation by competitor count and seriousness
cards.claim: In the speaker's product-research workflow, a product is more promising when no more than 10 stores are selling it and no more than three are serious competitors; stores that look awful or have stopped selling it are treated as green flags rather than serious competition.
cards.action: Use Magic AI to search a product, review the stores/competitors running it on Facebook, count total stores and serious competitors, and treat non-serious or abandoned stores as a green flag to start running the product.
applies_when: using a product research tool that shows Facebook competitors
do_not_use_when: the number of stores or seriousness of competitors cannot be verified
the tool does not show competitors running the product
unknowns: How to define a 'serious competitor' consistently
Whether the 10-store/3-serious-competitor thresholds generalize beyond this example
Whether the product has independent demand or only low observed competition
evidence_quotes: our goal here is that no more than 10 stores are selling it and that no more than three are serious competitors.
he's not a very serious competitor. The store looks absolutely awful.
they're not even selling it anymore. So what that would mean in this situation is that it's a pretty green flag to start running it.

cards.title: Daily product research pipeline in a Google Sheet
cards.claim: The speaker recommends tracking favorites in a Google Sheet, optionally including competitor pages, buy price, intended selling price, and notes; each day add three products, narrow to three favorites, then pick one favorite to run.
cards.action: Create a Google Sheet for product research, add three products per day, reduce the list to three favorites, choose one favorite from those three, and run that product.
applies_when: managing a pipeline of product candidates
do_not_use_when: unable to track buy price or intended selling price
unknowns: What criteria should determine the three favorites
How long to test the chosen product
Whether the daily three-product cadence is suitable for every operator

cards.title: Blue-ocean audience targeting for saturated products
cards.claim: The speaker argues that saturation indicates demand, and that a product can be given new life by finding an untapped audience; blue oceans are identified by researching the product, finding competitors, and seeing what they are not doing.
cards.action: Search the product on TikTok, review competitor marketing, identify audiences or angles competitors are not targeting, and adapt the marketing to that untapped audience.
applies_when: the product is saturated but appears to have demand
an untargeted audience segment can be identified
do_not_use_when: no evidence of product demand exists
the new audience/angle cannot be validated
unknowns: How to validate that the untapped audience will buy
Whether claims such as 'pretty much 100% success rate' in an untapped country are reliable
How broadly the shoe-dryer and home-workout examples apply
evidence_quotes: when the product is saturated, it only means one thing, demand, right?
Step two, identify blue oceans by researching a product, finding competitors, and seeing what they're not doing.
the easiest way to detect market opportunity is by searching up the product on Tik Tok.
So, step number one, find a product that solves a problem.
